hook: When you jump, you push down on the ground, yet you go up. When a rocket fires, it pushes gas backward and the rocket goes forward. Every force comes with a partner pushing the other way on the other object. Seeing those partners clearly is what lets you choose systems and ignore the forces inside them.

prereq.q: Every force on a free-body diagram has
options: the same size as the weight
a partner on the same diagram
prereq.why: A force is an interaction, so some object exerts it.

options: the objects you choose to study, inside a boundary
the object with the largest mass
prereq.why: You choose the system; the rest is the surroundings.

figure.caption: The two forces on the book are not partners. Each interaction gives a pair on two different objects.

chain.cause: Object A exerts a force on object B
chain.effect: B exerts a force on A of the same size, the opposite direction and the same type

chain.cause: The two partner forces act on different objects
chain.effect: they appear on different free-body diagrams and never cancel each other

chain.cause: Both objects are inside the system you chose
chain.effect: the pair are internal forces and add to zero for the system

chain.cause: Only external forces are left in the sum for the system
chain.effect: only external forces can change how the system's center of mass moves

ideas: Newton's third law: if A pushes on B, B pushes on A with a force equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type. Partners act on different objects.
To name a partner, swap the two objects and flip the direction: "road on tire, forward" ↔ "tire on road, backward".
Internal forces act between parts of the system and cancel in pairs; external forces come from the surroundings.
An ideal string is massless and does not stretch: one tension all along it. An ideal pulley is massless and frictionless: it turns the string without changing the tension.

misconception.wrong: The normal force and the weight of a book on a table are a third-law pair, because they are equal and opposite.
misconception.right: Both act on the book, so they cannot be partners. The weight's partner is the book pulling up on Earth; the normal force's partner is the book pushing down on the table.

summary: Forces come in third-law pairs: equal in size, opposite in direction, same type, acting on two different objects, so they never cancel each other. Inside a chosen system the pairs are internal and add to zero; an ideal string carries one tension over an ideal pulley.
